rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To cope with rejection and hurt, the Prophet should withdraw from those who reject truth, seek God’s mercy, and remember His name so God envelops him in mercy.
rows.anchor: on such occasions, he should cut himself off from people who do not value the truth and seek refuge with the mercy of his Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Keeping knowledge of God’s attributes fresh fortifies the believer against Satan, making him firm as a mountain.
rows.anchor: true knowledge of these attributes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Weak comprehension of divine attributes makes belief baseless or weak and leaves the believer vulnerable to every crisis.
rows.anchor: every outbreak of lightning striking his own shelter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is Lord of East and West alone; He has no partner, and no one can obstruct His intentions.
rows.anchor: no one can cause hindrance in the implementation of His intentions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Prophet makes God his guardian, God will suffice him, as also stated in 4:81.
rows.anchor: If the Prophet (sws) makes Him his guardian, He will suffice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should patiently bear opponents’ foolish speech, remain firm, avoid excessive pursuit, and ignore them with dignity.
rows.anchor: He should neither be sorrowful at what they say nor go after them too much; he should just ignore them in a dignified manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dignified abandonment serves reform and God’s pleasure, unlike humiliation and revenge; the righteous feel sorrow for those facing a terrible fate.
rows.anchor: people and to please their Lord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such noble conduct can move people with some goodness to examine themselves; the Prophet endures excesses until God decrees punishment, when separation precedes destruction.
rows.anchor: This dissociation is a prelude to their destruction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sternly warns the rejecters and tells the Prophet to leave them for God to deal with as He makes an example of them.
rows.anchor: he does not need to do anything.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day will bring the upheaval described in the verse, with the earth and mountains shaking and the mountains reduced to sand.
rows.anchor: This is a reminder of the day when the conceited people will face what is depicted in the verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the rejecters as affluent refers to the rich, while the related term for blessing means riches and affluence.
rows.anchor: means “riches and affluence.” By citing this attribute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their affluence is cited to expose denial’s cause and condemn ingratitude: God’s gift made them arrogant against Him.
rows.anchor: they should have been grateful to Him; on the contrary, this God-given affluence made them arrogant and haughty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fail to meet the obligation of their abundant food and resources will face food lodged in their throats and painful punishment.
rows.anchor: because of the copious food and resources they have been blessed with

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sent a Messenger to Quraysh to teach His directives, how to please Him, and the reward and fate tied to obedience or denial.
rows.anchor: they will earn in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger is a witness to truth and God judges right and wrong through him; Islahi explains this witness role through 2:143, and Pharaoh’s seizure warns Quraysh of their own fate.
rows.anchor: through him a judgement shall be passed regarding what is right and what is wrong.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day that makes children old is an idiom expressing the intensity and all-embracing nature of a horror.
rows.anchor: We often say: “That sorrow has made me grow old.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: Narratives report that the Prophet said Sūrah Hūd and similar sūrahs made him grow old.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab poets use this familiar idiom in various ways; Islahi cites examples from al-Zamakhsharī that he considers reliable.
rows.anchor: some examples which can be relied upon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden of the Day of Judgement weighs on the sky, which may split and reveal the Day suddenly while people remain heedless; 7:187 likewise says it burdens heaven and earth and comes suddenly.
rows.anchor: The heavens and the earth are burdened with it. It will come upon you suddenly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although only God knows the Hereafter’s time, its signs are obvious like a pregnancy near delivery, so it may arrive at any time.
rows.anchor: everyone who sees her knows that she will deliver

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People are unfortunate to ignore the Hereafter merely because its exact arrival time is unknown.
rows.anchor: Unfortunate are people who are indifferent to it merely because its exact time of arrival is not known to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This” refers to Qur’anic verses warning Quraysh about the Hereafter; the warning leaves them no excuse because the truth reached them in its ultimate form.
rows.anchor: The demonstrative pronoun “this” refers to those verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the warning, each person is responsible for choosing the path to the Lord and His mercy or remaining in error and facing the outcome.
rows.anchor: It was now the responsibility of the people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though its subject indicates a Madinan revelation, the final verse returns to the night-prayer directive at the sūrah’s beginning, linking its opening and close; this arrangement reflects guidance from God and His Prophet.
rows.anchor: it was placed at the end of this sūrah so that one is able to understand the relationship between the initial and final directives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse praises the Prophet for fulfilling night prayer, which God knows and will reward.
rows.anchor: these endeavours of his are in the knowledge of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also praises Companions who voluntarily adopted the Prophet’s tahajjud practice as mandatory for themselves and eagerly followed his example.
rows.anchor: the Companions who in their fervour to follow him adopted the tahajjud prayer as a mandatory practice of their own accord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night-prayer directive specifically addressed the Prophet; although faith calls believers to follow him, their lesser endurance required God to ease the burden for ordinary Muslims.
rows.anchor: there is a world of difference between the power of endurance of a prophet and that of common people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone measures night and day, knows people’s circumstances, and judges that the Companions cannot sustain the specified night-prayer fractions, so they should recite what they can.
rows.anchor: the Companions will not be able to stand up in prayer for half the night or one third or two thirds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the verb tāba, the preposition ʿalā gives the sense “to turn to someone graciously.”
rows.anchor: it means “to turn to someone graciously.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general instruction to recite as much as possible refers here to Qur’an recitation in tahajjud; measured recitation in that prayer brings special blessings, though recitation itself is rewarding.
rows.anchor: reading it in a measured tone in the tahajjud prayer brings the blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Relief was given because ordinary Muslims could not sustain the taxing directive; the Prophet continued it until death, while for others tahajjud remains optional and its length follows their zeal.
rows.anchor: he abided by this directive till his very last breath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Journeys for a noble cause include seeking knowledge, performing hajj, or doing business.
rows.anchor: every journey which is undertaken for a noble and higher cause whether it is for seeking knowledge or for offering the ḥajj or for doing business

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To compensate for less night prayer, Muslims should maintain the five prayers diligently and spend for God’s cause, including supporting His word and urgent religious or state needs.
rows.anchor: to compensate for not being able to pray the tahajjud

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Generous spending can mean any charitable spending, but alongside zakāh it denotes expenditure for war or an emergency need.
rows.anchor: for the requirements of war or for some emergency need

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending for God’s cause benefits the believers themselves, is credited to their accounts with God, and is the most profitable trade.
rows.anchor: this spending is not an unprofitable undertaking

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alongside the other duties, believers should seek forgiveness for their faults and hope for God’s forgiveness and mercy.
rows.anchor: believers should continue to seek forgiveness from their Lord for their sins and faults

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The affluent man’s expectation of receiving more is false, and if he opposes the Qur’an he faces a severe penalty.
rows.anchor: This, it is clear, is a totally false claim.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant Quraysh leader fashioned a disdainfully delivered excuse, misjudging the Qur’an as a prophet’s stirring eloquence and ignoring its warning, though its statements are realities he will soon meet.
rows.anchor: they reckoned it to be a miracle of a prophet’s stirring and eloquent speech and never paid attention to its warning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers mock the description of Hell because they presume to know everything, but it rests on divine wisdom: truth-seekers benefit and arrogant know-it-alls ruin their fate.
rows.anchor: Those who have the desire for the truth will benefit from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nature’s manifestations argue for the Hereafter and expose heedlessness; the Qur’an warns so people can prepare, while evaders are left with stubbornness as their excuse.
rows.anchor: An argument on the Hereafter from the manifestations of nature is presented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each soul is held for its own deeds, and only its deeds can free it or lead it to Hell; neither another’s deeds nor intercession benefits someone else.
rows.anchor: each person will be held in pledge for his own deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of the right hand are the victors in Paradise and ask those in Hell what brought them there; the latter openly confess their crimes.
rows.anchor: the crimes which led them to their state of doom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s fleeing audience has an indicated underlying motive; the Prophet should ignore them and only remind them, while benefit is reserved for those God’s laws make receptive.
rows.anchor: deserve to benefit from it

none: Qur’anic text and its translation only.
Qur’anic text and translation only; no commentary in this segment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to rise and warn launches the assignment foreshadowed by 73:5: the Prophet must openly warn his people with resolve despite opposition, trusting God to ease his way and strengthen him.
rows.anchor: He should arise and with full determination and resolve, warn his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the “heavy word” of 73:5 as the burden of public warning, not revelation itself, since revelations had already begun; proclaiming tawḥīd and threatened punishment to Makkah’s and Ṭā’if’s leaders was onerous.
rows.anchor: the burden of a heavy word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “heavy word” of 73:5 refers to the duty to deliver open warning to the Prophet’s people.
rows.anchor: referred to in the previous verse by the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first warning directive is monotheism: because the object precedes the verb, proclaiming greatness is specified for God alone; every other claim to greatness is false.
rows.anchor: Since the object of the verb in this verse has been placed before the verb, it has resulted in specifying this declaration for God only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In pagan Arabia, proclaiming God’s sole greatness provoked society, yet every prophet had to declare tawḥīd openly because it is religion’s foundation.
rows.anchor: every prophet was required to openly declare it without showing any hesitation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thiyāb normally means clothing but can metaphorically mean the heart’s apparel; Islahi cites Imru’u al-Qays’s verse using it for the heart and his line describing Banū ʿAwf’s hearts as clean.
rows.anchor: and you will be separated from me.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command means that the Prophet must keep his heart free of shirk and proclaim tawḥīd without fear; it rejects Quraysh’s later compromise offer to recognize their deities, as 68:9 also addresses.
rows.anchor: he should not compromise in any way in this matter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijz, rijs, and rijz have similar sounds and meanings; here rijz means the repellent filth of polytheism, reinforcing the prior command to purify the heart.
rows.anchor: used for the filth which makes a person feel abhorrence and disgust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purity command was not needed because the Prophet was never at risk of shirk; it tells idolaters that their warner has a clear, firm monotheist stance and divine instructions.
rows.anchor: to communicate to the disbelievers and the idolaters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must continue the divinely assigned preaching and warning until God tells him to stop, rather than thinking he has done enough; the relevant root can mean favor or cut, as 68:3 illustrates.
rows.anchor: not discontinue it thinking that he has done it to a great extent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some reciters use jazm, Islahi prefers the mutawātir ḍammah reading of tastakthir; he takes it as a circumstantial accusative rather than an independent sentence.
rows.anchor: I would prefer to read it thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istikthār can mean doing or wanting much or counting something as much; though 7:188 uses the first sense, Islahi prefers “regard as much” here, following the lexicographic sense listed first in Aqrab al-mawārid.
rows.anchor: to regard or reckon something to be a lot
